title: onprem-hybrid-connectivity-play-notes
content:
Purpose / context:
This is a working playbook for small-to-medium POCs where the customer needs hybrid connectivity between Redwood Private (control plane or inference nodes) and customer-managed on-prem or cross-account VPCs. Focus: practical, lowest-friction options (networking and DNS) plus tests and rollback steps. Not a canonical enterprise design (that lives in private-deployments design docs); this is the fast path used by SEs during discovery workshops and POC setup.

Summary recommendations (short):
- Prefer AWS Transit Gateway (TGW) or cloud vendor equivalent when multiple VPCs / on-prem exist or when transit/transitive routing is required.
- For single-VPC direct connects, use VPC peering + NAT + managed endpoints only if you can accept peering limitations (no transitive).
- Always offer a split-horizon DNS plan: private hosted zone + conditional forwarders to on-prem DNS.
- Use VPC endpoints for cloud storage control plane traffic (S3, Secrets Manager) and avoid egress to the internet for control traffic.
- For early POC, use a symmetric design: outbound-only traffic from on-prem to Redwood with mTLS and IP allowlist; defer inbound public endpoints unless necessary.

Design patterns (tradeoffs):
1) Direct VPC peering (fastest to set up for single customer VPC)
   - Pros: simple, no extra infra, low latency.
   - Cons: not transitive; route table management becomes painful with many peers; cross-account peering requires accept step.
   - When to use: single customer VPC, <2 additional networks, short-lived POC.

2) Transit Gateway / Cloud Router (recommended when scale or on-prem present)
   - Pros: supports transitive routing, centralised route control, easier multi-VPC+onprem connectivity.
   - Cons: cost and slightly more complex setup; requires TGW attachment and route propagation.
   - When to use: multi-VPC architectures, long-running POCs, or when BGP/Direct Connect exists.

3) Private egress with NAT + proxy (egress-through-redwood)
   - Use case: customer wants no public egress from inference clusters.
   - Pattern: deploy NAT Gateway (or egress proxy) in VPC; create security policy to allow outbound to Redwood control plane IP ranges or private endpoint.
   - Note: watch for SNAT port exhaustion with high concurrent flows; recommend using ALB/ENI-backed nat solutions or proxy pooling.

DNS patterns and common pitfalls:
- Split-horizon DNS (recommended): create private hosted zone for redwood.private.example (or customer-specific zone). For on-prem resolution, configure conditional forwarder to the nearest CoreDNS instance or on-prem DNS server.
- Stub zones: useful if customer insists on authoritative on-prem names. Use forwarders in cloud DNS to on-prem DNS IPs over the VPN/Direct Connect.
- Avoid relying on public names for internal endpoints. Example bug: customer uses external load balancer hostname in config; during failover the LB IP changes and TLS certs break.
- CoreDNS example (K8s) to forward customer.local to on-prem DNS:
  - snippet:
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: ConfigMap
    data:
      Corefile: |
        .:53 {
          errors
          health
          kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
            pods insecure
            fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
          }
          forward . /etc/resolv.conf
        }
        customer.local:53 {
          forward . 10.10.1.2
        }

Endpoints and private connectivity checklist (POC quick checklist):
- Identify required outbound ports and destinations (control plane, S3, KMS, metrics endpoints).
- Decide: do we need inbound routes to customer network? If yes, document source IPs and ports; prefer private endpoint behind VPN.
- Create security groups with explicit CIDR ranges or prefix-lists.
- If using TGW, confirm route propagation between attachments and enforce blackhole detection.
- Configure VPC endpoints for S3 and Secrets Manager; validate IAM role policies for endpoint usage.
- For on-prem VPN: test MTU and fragmentation thresholds.

Firewall / routing gotchas we've tripped on:
- AWS VPC peering is not transitive: customer often tries to route through their transit VPC expecting transitive; catch this early.
- ICMP blocked by default by security groups; our healthchecks may fail if not allowed.
- Asymmetric routing with NAT gateways can break source-based firewall rules on-prem. Use sticky source NAT or proxy to stabilize source IPs.
- BGP route flaps on Direct Connect can cause route withdraws on TGW; set community tags and dampening if available.

Security and compliance notes:
- KMS: ensure encryption keys are accessible to the appropriate account/role; prefer cross-account grants over sharing keys.
- Audit logs: enable VPC flow logs to central logging bucket/ELK; redact token fields in logs before sharing with customers.
- Least privilege: tighten SGs to only known Redwood control-plane IP prefixes or use PrivateLink endpoints where possible.
- Bring-your-own-certs: discuss termination point (ALB vs on-prem TLS terminator). For HIPAA/PCI customers, prefer TLS to the edge and no cleartext on internal network.

Operational runbook (POC deploy -> rollback):
- Pre-flight (1-2 days before): collect VPC IDs, route tables, CIDRs, DNS server IPs, owner contacts, and expected flows. Create ephemeral test VMs in customer VPCs.
- Deploy phase:
  1) Establish VPN or Direct Connect.
  2) Attach TGW or peer VPCs.
  3) Configure route tables and security groups.
  4) Deploy CoreDNS forwarder and test resolution.
  5) Configure VPC endpoints and validate S3 access.
  6) Validate TLS/mTLS handshakes and certs.
- Smoke tests (example):
  - curl https://control-plane.internal/health -> 200
  - dig _service._tcp.customer.local -> SRV entries as expected
  - traceroute to control plane from on-prem bastion (<= 6 hops typical)
  - s3 list-only via VPC endpoint (no public egress)
- Rollback (fast): revert route table to previous state, remove TGW attachment, delete peering. Maintain change window and keep configuration backups.

Measurement and evals for POC success criteria:
- Latency: 95th percentile RTT from on-prem to inference node <= 50ms (adjust for geography)
- Egress stability: no more than 1% packet loss during test window
- Auth: Mutual TLS handshake success rate >= 99% across 1k connections
- Cost: List estimated TGW + Data Transfer for 30-day run, compare to peering + NAT baseline.

Customer questions to ask in initial workshop (short list):
- Do you have an existing TGW or backbone? Any required route policies?
- Are there IP ranges we must avoid (overlapping subnets)?
- Is traffic primarily outbound from your environment to Redwood, or do you need inbound connections?
- What DNS servers are authoritative for internal names? Can we add conditional forwarders?
- Are there strict egress rules for S3 or external logging endpoints?

Open decisions / TODOs (work-in-progress):
- Decide if we should publish canonical prefix-list for Redwood control plane IPs (helps customers write SGs) — engineering to confirm.
- Investigate automating CoreDNS conditional forwarder deployment as part of the POC helm chart (ticket SE-5039).
- Confirm the recommended NAT sizing guidance for 1k concurrent clients (ops owner: Miguel).

Notes from the last customer workshop (2025-11-12):
- Customer wants no public IPs on inference nodes; insisted on private-only egress. We validated VPC endpoint approach but they need verification from their security team re: S3 endpoint policies.
- On-prem DNS team prefers conditional forwarder over split-horizon; they will provide DNS server IPs and credentials for a short test window.

Appendix: quick example route table entries (AWS)
- TGW attached to account A, propagate to VPC attachment: 10.10.0.0/16 -> tgw-attach-0a, 10.20.0.0/16 -> tgw-attach-0b
- Peering route: 10.30.0.0/16 -> pcx-12345

Common troubleshooting commands:
- AWS: aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters "Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-xxxx"
- traceroute from bastion -> identify hop where path diverges
- tcpdump on ENI to confirm NAT vs direct source IPs
- dig +trace customer.local @<onprem-dns>

Contact/owners for this playbook: Claire Donovan (SE lead), Miguel Ortega (infra ops).
